summary: The Risk Lab makes the scoring rulebook hands-on: toggle signals, or pick a preset story, and the real engine scores the combination. Signals, weights, levels and thresholds all come from `GET /risk/rules`, and every change is sent to `POST /risk/evaluate`, a dry run that stores nothing and uses the same scoring code as the ingestion pipeline. The result is shown as a gauge, a level badge, a waterfall of contributions and a written formula.

notes.text: Header comment: the page calls the real engine through `POST /risk/evaluate`, but nothing is stored, so it is a safe sandbox for exploring the rulebook.
API helpers and DOM helpers, including `$$` (querySelectorAll returning an array) and `debounce`.
Motion helpers for card presses, staggered effects and the entrance.
The semicircle `gauge` and the score `waterfall`, the same charts used in the drawers and the Simulation Center.
MITRE ATT&CK link, panel frame, severity badge and `icon`.

Preset stories as `[name, signals]` pairs, from harmless to hostile; the names must match the backend's signal names exactly, because the request schema `EvaluateIn` rejects unknown ones. The first three score LOW, LOW and MEDIUM, and **Clean login** sums to −15, which is clamped up to 0.
The attack presets all land in CRITICAL. **Account takeover** sums to 125 (40 + 30 + 15 + 10 + 30), so it also demonstrates the clamp down to 100.
Page module titled `Risk Lab`. Like Customers, it has no live data or timers, so `render` doesn't take `ctx`.

Fetches the rulebook: every signal (name, weight, description and ATT&CK mapping), the levels with their actions, and the detection thresholds. The page is built entirely from it, so changing a weight in `rules.py` changes the Lab without any frontend edit.
The selected signals, kept in a `Set` (no duplicates, fast lookups). It starts with New device + Unusual location (15 + 20 = 35, MEDIUM), so the first view already shows an interesting result.
A short alias for the thresholds object used throughout the markup.
Mounts the page markup.
Header explaining the model: a score is a plain sum of weighted signals, clamped to 0-100.
The left column (7 of the 12 grid columns) starts with one button per preset and a ghost `Clear` button, whose empty `data-preset` matches no preset.
One toggle card per rulebook signal. `aria-pressed` tells assistive technology whether the card is on (CSS styles pressed cards too), and the top row shows a check mark and the signal name.

The weight with an explicit `+` for positive values (negative numbers already carry a minus sign, plus a `neg` class for styling), the description and, when mapped, a MITRE ATT&CK link. The last line closes the left column.
Right column (5 grid columns): the **Engine output** panel, starting with the empty `data-gauge` slot where the gauge is drawn.
Three more empty slots that `evaluate` fills: the level badge (centred), the waterfall and the written formula. The last line closes the first grid row.
**Levels & actions** panel: a ruler listing each level, its minimum score and the action the engine recommends, all read from the rulebook.

**Detection thresholds** panel, also driven by the API: how many failed attempts trigger a signal, and the speed above which travel counts as impossible. The `>` entity is needed because the static text of a template is raw HTML.
The minimum distance before travel is judged at all (shorter hops are within geo-IP noise), the rapid-transaction velocity rule and the password-spray rule.
The large-transaction amount formatted as US dollars, the score that opens an incident and the correlation window. The last line closes the panel and the template.

The last score shown, so the gauge can animate **from** it. Toggling a +20 signal moves the needle up by 20 instead of sweeping up from zero every time, which makes each signal's effect easy to see. `latest` numbers the requests, so a stale answer can be recognized.
`evaluate` scores the current selection.
Takes a ticket: toggling quickly sends several requests, and only the newest may draw.
`evaluate` sends the selected signal names to `POST /risk/evaluate`. The server scores them with the same functions the ingestion pipeline uses.
A response overtaken by a newer toggle is dropped. Sometimes it used to land last and leave the gauge showing a selection that was no longer current.
Redraws the gauge, animating from `previous` to the new score, then remembers the new score for next time.
Shows the level badge and the waterfall of contributions. `showDetail: false` hides each row's detail line, which for a dry run would only repeat the signal description already printed on the card.
Builds the formula terms, writing negative weights with a typographic minus (`− 15`), and the raw sum before clamping.

Writes the formula, for example `15 + 20 = 35 → MEDIUM · Monitor and log`. The regex turns `+ −` into a plain `−`, an extra `→ clamp →` step appears only when the sum fell outside 0-100, and the level is shown in its colour. The last line closes `evaluate`.
A debounced version of `evaluate`: rapid clicking sends one request, 90 ms after the last change, instead of one per click.
`sync` copies the `Set` into each card's `aria-pressed`. The Set is the single source of truth and the DOM only mirrors it.
One delegated click listener. For a signal card it ignores clicks on the card's ATT&CK link, so opening the reference doesn't also toggle the signal.
Toggles the signal in the Set (a ternary used as a statement) and syncs the cards.
Gives the card a small springy press (`scale` 0.97 to 1) and asks for a fresh score.
When a preset button was clicked, the current selection is cleared first.
Adds the chosen preset's signals. `?.[1]` reads the matching preset's signal list; `Clear` (an empty name) matches nothing and falls back to an empty array.
Syncs the cards and pops every now-pressed card in a quick 40 ms stagger, so the user sees which signals the preset switched on.
Requests the new score, then closes the preset branch and the listener.
Staggered fade-up of the signal cards when the page opens.
Scores the default selection straight away. Because it is awaited, `render` (and with it the router's progress bar) finishes only once the first result is drawn.
Closes `render` and the page object.
